caller_shapes.header_form: the record pointer itself (rdi = rbx at 0x474dbf0); no header lea exists

pair_verdict: One pair-destroy call destroys exactly one element.  The arguments are the element's two words: rdi = the data word, rsi = the descriptor word (a pointer to the 0x18-byte descriptor record).  The helper saves both, then: (1) descriptor word 0 ([rsi+0x0]) is called on the data when non-null (call at 0x1537b16 / 0x474e0c6); (2) the size word ([rsi+0x8]) is tested -- when zero the helper simply returns; when non-zero the dealloc class is computed from the align word ([rsi+0x10]) by the same tzcnt/cmov idiom as the drains (tzcnt at 0x1537b25 / 0x474e0d5; class 0 when align <= size, the tzcnt when align > size, and the tzcnt whenever align >= 0x11), the registers are restored, and the data is freed through the dealloc slot 0x64df4a0 (RELATIVE target 0x635de30) as a TAIL JUMP (0x1537b41 / 0x474e0f1) with (data, size, class).  Order is descriptor call first, free second -- the normal drains' per-element order.  There is no loop in the helper: the iteration over the remaining elements lives in the drain landing pads (counter dec at 0x153df70 / 0x474e960, cursor advancing 0x10, one helper call per element at 0x153df83 / 0x474e973).  Unwind behaviour: the helper's own landing pad (+0x4d) saves the exception, re-runs the same size/class computation and frees the data through the slot in CALL form (0x1537b74 / 0x474e124) when the size word is non-zero, then calls _Unwind_Resume (PLT 0x63f0a50) with the saved exception.
clone_verdict: The two helpers are clones at the pinned instruction shape, judged by the #2714 method (unmasked instruction diff + consumption order).  Both decode to 44 instructions at identical offsets and, after masking the address-dependent tails, byte-identical streams.  The unmasked difference is exactly three sites, each a 4-byte displacement field, and every one resolves to the SAME shared target in both instances: the tail jump's RIP-relative displacement (offset 0x41) and the pad free's RIP-relative displacement (offset 0x74) both name the dealloc slot 0x64df4a0, and the resume call's rel32 (offset 0x7d) names the shared _Unwind_Resume PLT 0x63f0a50.  Unlike the drain pairs -- whose five and four differences each include a module-local call target -- NO difference here resolves to a module-local target: the helpers call nothing of their own module (the descriptor function is indirect through the descriptor, the free goes through the shared slot, the resume through the shared PLT).  The bodies' own hashes differ, as the pinned records show; identity is claimed at the masked instruction shape only.
family_verdict: The four caller FDEs of the 86-byte wrappers are not themselves wrappers and are not mutual clones (258 / 699 / 258 / 230 bytes; the two element drops are clones of each other per #2714, the two record destructors are not clones of anything).  Each of the four is a record destructor that embeds the same two-half drain-and-free pattern over its record's sub-vector header, at the pinned sites in caller_shapes: NORMAL half -- call the module's normal drain on the header, then free the buffer inline: capacity word (header +0x0) loaded, gated non-zero, buffer pointer (header +0x8), size = capacity << 4, align 0, through the dealloc slot 0x64df4a0.  UNWIND half -- a landing pad that protects the fields destroyed before the drain call routes the same header through the 86-byte drain+free wrapper (exactly one wrapper call per caller FDE, all in pad blocks), while a landing pad that protects the drain call itself re-runs only the inline buffer free (the drain has already consumed the elements, so the wrapper's drain half must not run again).  The 86-byte body is therefore the shared out-of-line unwind half of one pattern that every wrapper caller embeds -- the whole drop path in each module is generated from this one pattern, with the wrapper as its unwind form.  Two measured deviations: (a) the vec-A record destructor 0x1538460 performs the normal-path free as a slot CALL at 0x1538570 (further fields follow), where the other three callers use the epilogue tail-jump form after restoring registers; (b) the reader record destructor 0x474dba0 has its header at record +0x0 -- the record pointer itself is passed to both drain and wrapper, and its first field is an inline pair-destroy of the tagged pair at record +0x18/+0x20 (descriptor call 0x474dbbf, tzcnt 0x474dbd0, dealloc call 0x474dbe7, re-run on the pad at 0x474dc4d) -- where the other three callers pass record +0x18 as the header.
census_verdict: Transfer census over the whole .text (E8 calls and E9 tail jumps, sites attributed by containing FDE): each pair-destroy helper has exactly ONE direct caller -- its own module's normal-drain landing-pad loop (0x153df83 in 0x153deb0; 0x474e973 in 0x474e8a0) -- and no tail-jump caller exists for either helper or for either wrapper.  Each 86-byte wrapper has exactly the two callers the drain packet recorded (the element drop's first landing pad and the record destructor's pad, per module).  No other direct caller of any of the four exists in the binary.
limits: Static trace only.  Hash-pinned, not traced: the two normal drains and the two 86-byte wrappers (traced by the drain-callees packet, retained here as boundary context), the dealloc target 0x635de30, and _Unwind_Resume.  Caller shapes are pinned at the drain/free/wrapper sites listed in caller_shapes; the remaining fields of the two record destructors (strings, tagged pairs, the tag-3 dispatch in 0x1538460) are not traced, and which landing pad protects which call range is identified by pad content and position, not by re-decoding the LSDA.  What the elements' descriptor drop functions do beyond the call, and any semantic name for the element or record types, are not claimed.  No captured code executed, no runtime value or reconstruction gate is claimed.
